transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A new study has found that eating breakfast every day may improve children's academic performance and help them do better in school, according to researchers at the University of Iowa. The study followed over 5,000 elementary school students and found that those who ate breakfast every day scored significantly higher on math, reading, and science tests than those who skipped breakfast or only ate it sometimes. The researchers say that breakfast provides the brain with energy after a night of fasting, and it improves concentration, memory, and attention span. They also note that children who eat breakfast are more likely to have better overall nutrition and are less likely to be overweight. The study's authors say that ensuring all children have access to a healthy breakfast could be an effective way to improve educational outcomes, especially for low-income children who may not have regular access to breakfast at home.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the University of Iowa study find about breakfast?
2. Why might breakfast help children do better in school?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The city of Amsterdam has announced plans to ban all gasoline and diesel cars and motorcycles from the city center by 2030, as part of its efforts to reduce air pollution and become a more sustainable city. The ban will be phased in gradually, starting with older, more polluting vehicles in 2025, and eventually including all fossil fuel-powered vehicles by 2030. The city says that the ban will significantly improve air quality, reduce noise pollution, and make the city center safer and more pleasant for pedestrians and cyclists. Amsterdam already has one of the highest rates of cycling in the world, and the city plans to invest even more in cycling infrastructure, public transportation, and electric vehicle charging stations to make the transition easier. Critics say the ban will be inconvenient for drivers and will hurt businesses in the city center, but supporters say the health benefits of cleaner air far outweigh the costs.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What has Amsterdam announced?
4. What is one benefit of the ban mentioned in the passage?
5. What is one criticism of the ban?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Researchers at MIT have developed a new type of self-reconfiguring robot that can change its shape and form by assembling and disassembling itself from small, identical modular units. The robot is made up of small cube-shaped modules that can move independently, attach to and detach from each other, and work together to form different shapes and structures. Unlike traditional robots that are built for a single purpose, these modular robots can adapt to different tasks and environments by changing their shape—they can form a rolling wheel to move across flat ground, a snake-like shape to crawl through tight spaces, or a climbing structure to go over obstacles. Researchers say this type of flexible, adaptable robot could be useful in many situations, from search and rescue operations in disaster zones to space exploration to construction. The technology is still in the early stages, but researchers are working on making the modules smaller, smarter, and more capable.

7. What is one potential use mentioned for the technology?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Chloe): Hey Alex, I heard you're looking for a new apartment. How's the search going?

Man (Alex): Ugh, it's going terribly. I've been looking for weeks and I can't find anything that's not either way too expensive or way too small or in a terrible neighborhood. I'm starting to think I'll never find anything.
Woman: Yeah, apartment hunting is the worst. I remember how stressed I was when I was looking for my place. What are you looking for exactly? Maybe I can help.

Man: Well, I need a one-bedroom apartment, preferably with a separate kitchen. And it has to be close to the university—within walking distance or a short bus ride. My budget is about $800 a month, including bills if possible.
Woman: Hmm, $800 for a one-bedroom near the university... that might be tough. Rent has gone up a lot in this area lately.
Man: Yeah, I know. That's the problem. Everything I've seen so far is at least $900 or $1000, and that's not even including bills. I can't afford that.
Woman: Have you considered looking a bit further from the university? Rent is cheaper if you're willing to commute a bit.
Man: I don't know... I don't want to have to take the bus for 45 minutes every day. And public transport isn't that reliable here.
Woman: That's fair. What about getting a roommate? If you get a two-bedroom place with a roommate, you could split the rent and get a nicer place for less money.
Man: I thought about that, but I've never lived with a roommate before. I'm kind of used to having my own space. And what if I get a weird roommate?
Woman: Yeah, that's a risk. But it can also be really fun. I lived with a roommate my first two years of university and we had a great time. And you can save a lot of money.
Man: I guess. But how do you even find a good roommate?

Woman: There are websites and Facebook groups for people looking for roommates. You can meet people first and see if you get along before you decide to live together. And you should definitely check references and meet in person first.
Man: Hmm, maybe. What else? Have you seen any good places lately?

Woman: Actually, my neighbor is moving out next month. Her apartment is really nice—one bedroom, separate kitchen, decent size. It's on the third floor of a building about a 15-minute walk from campus. I think she said the rent is $850 a month, not including bills.
Man: $850... that's a bit over my budget, but maybe I could afford it if bills aren't too high. What's the building like?

Woman: It's pretty nice. It's an older building, but it's well maintained. There's a laundry room in the basement, and the landlord is really responsive when something breaks. The neighborhood is quiet and safe, and there are shops and cafes nearby.
Man: That sounds good. Do you think I could see it?
Woman: Sure! I can talk to my neighbor and see if she'd be okay with showing it to you. She's looking for someone to take over her lease, so you wouldn't have to wait long.
Man: That would be amazing! Thank you so much, Chloe. You're a lifesaver.
Woman: No problem! Let me text her and see when she's free. I'm sure she'd be happy to show it to you.
Man: Great. Fingers crossed it works out! I'm so tired of looking at apartments.
Woman: I know the feeling. Hopefully this one works out and you can stop stressing about it.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Leo): Hey Mia, I saw you in the art studio yesterday. I didn't know you painted! That's really cool.
Woman (Mia): Oh, thanks! Yeah, I've been painting for a few years now. It's just a hobby, but I really love it.
Man: That's awesome. How did you get into painting?

Woman: Well, I've always been interested in art, but I never really tried it myself until a couple of years ago. I was going through a really stressful time at work, and a friend suggested I try painting as a way to relax. I thought it sounded silly at first, but I gave it a try and I was hooked immediately.
Man: That's great. I've always wanted to try painting, but I'm terrible at art. I can't even draw a stick figure properly.
Woman: Oh, come on, that's not true! And even if you are bad at it at first, that's okay. It's not about being good—it's about having fun and relaxing. Everyone starts somewhere.
Man: I guess. But I don't even know where to start. There are so many different types of paint and brushes and canvases... it's overwhelming.

Woman: It can be overwhelming at first, but you don't need a ton of supplies to start. Just get some basic acrylic paints, a few brushes, and some canvas paper or a cheap canvas. Acrylics are great for beginners because they're easy to work with, they dry fast, and you can paint over mistakes easily.
Man: Acrylics? What about watercolors or oil paints?

Woman: Watercolors are beautiful but they're harder to control, especially for beginners. Oil paints are great but they take forever to dry and they're more expensive and messy. Acrylics are the most beginner-friendly, in my opinion.
Man: Okay, acrylics it is. What else do I need?

Woman: Just a few basic brushes—different sizes, some flat and some round. And maybe a palette to mix paint on. You can use an old plate or even a piece of cardboard if you don't want to buy a real palette.
Man: That doesn't sound too bad. But what do I paint? I have no ideas.

Woman: Start with something simple. Like a landscape—sky, mountains, a lake. Or just paint abstract shapes and colors. It doesn't have to be anything specific. The point is just to have fun and experiment. You can also follow tutorials online—there are tons of free painting tutorials on YouTube for beginners.
Man: That's a good idea. I'll have to check those out. Do you ever sell your paintings or show them anywhere?

Woman: Sometimes. I've sold a few to friends and family, and I've had a couple of pieces in local art shows. But I don't do it for the money—I just do it because I enjoy it. It's nice when people like my work, but even if no one ever saw it, I'd still paint.
Man: That's really cool. I wish I had a creative hobby like that.
Woman: You can! You should just try it. Come over to my place sometime and we can paint together. I have extra supplies you can use, and I can show you the basics. No pressure, just for fun.
Man: Really? That would be awesome! I'd love to try it.
Woman: Great! How about next Saturday afternoon? We can get some coffee, put on some music, and paint. It'll be fun.
Man: Perfect! I'm actually really excited about it. Thanks for offering to teach me.
Woman: No problem! It'll be fun. And remember—there's no such thing as a bad painting when you're just having fun.

13. What type of paint does Mia recommend for beginners?

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The Industrial Revolution was one of the most important periods in human history, transforming society from an agricultural economy based on farming and hand production to an industrial economy based on machine manufacturing and factory work. It began in Britain in the late 18th century and spread to other parts of Europe and North America over the next century, changing almost every aspect of daily life.

Before the Industrial Revolution, most people lived in small villages and worked on farms. Production was slow and done by hand, often in people's homes in what was called the "cottage industry." But starting in the textile industry, new inventions and technologies revolutionized production. The spinning jenny, the power loom, and other machines made it possible to produce cloth much faster and cheaper than ever before. Instead of working at home, people moved to factories where they worked long hours for wages.

The invention of the steam engine by James Watt was one of the most important developments of the Industrial Revolution. Steam power replaced water power and human and animal power, and it was used to run factories, power steamships, and drive locomotives on the new railways. Railroads and steamships transformed transportation, making it faster and cheaper to move goods and people over long distances.

The Industrial Revolution had enormous effects on society. Cities grew rapidly as people moved from rural areas to work in factories, creating the first large industrial cities. But these early industrial cities were often crowded, dirty, and unhealthy, with poor working and living conditions. Factory work was dangerous and hours were long, especially for women and children who often worked for very low pay.

Over time, however, the Industrial Revolution also brought many benefits. It increased productivity and created wealth, leading to a higher standard of living for many people. It led to advances in technology, medicine, and science. And it laid the foundation for the modern industrialized world we live in today.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Bees and other pollinators like butterflies, bats, and birds play a crucial role in our ecosystem and our food supply, yet many populations are declining rapidly around the world due to habitat loss, pesticide use, climate change, and disease. Understanding why pollinators are important is essential for protecting them and ensuring food security for future generations.

Pollination is the process by which pollen is transferred from the male part of a flower to the female part, allowing the plant to produce fruit and seeds. While some plants are pollinated by wind or water, about 75 percent of the world's flowering plants and more than 35 percent of global food crops depend on animal pollinators to reproduce. That means one out of every three bites of food we eat exists because of pollinators.

Bees are the most well-known and important pollinators. There are over 20,000 species of bees around the world, including honeybees, bumblebees, and solitary bees. Honeybees are the most commonly managed pollinators, and beekeepers move hives around to pollinate crops like almonds, apples, and blueberries. But wild bees are also extremely important, and in many cases they're even more effective pollinators than honeybees.

Unfortunately, pollinator populations are declining at an alarming rate. In many parts of the world, bee populations have dropped by 30 to 50 percent in recent decades. There are several reasons for this decline. Habitat loss is a major factor—as natural areas are converted to agriculture and urban development, pollinators lose the flowers they feed on and the places they nest. Pesticides, especially a class called neonicotinoids, are also harmful to bees and can kill them or impair their ability to navigate and reproduce.

The loss of pollinators is a serious problem. Without them, we would lose many of the fruits, vegetables, and nuts that make our diets healthy and varied. We would also lose many wild plants, which would have cascading effects throughout entire ecosystems.

But there are things we can do to help. Planting native flowers and creating pollinator-friendly gardens provides food and habitat for bees and other pollinators. Reducing pesticide use and supporting organic farming also helps. And raising awareness about the importance of pollinators can lead to policy changes that protect them.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Volunteering—giving your time and energy to help others without being paid—has been shown to have numerous benefits for both the people receiving help and the volunteers themselves. While most people volunteer because they want to make a difference and help their communities, research has shown that volunteering can also improve the volunteer's physical and mental health, social connections, and even career prospects.

One of the most well-documented benefits of volunteering is its positive effect on mental health. Helping others and contributing to something bigger than yourself gives people a sense of purpose and meaning, which can reduce feelings of depression and anxiety. Volunteering also provides social connection and reduces loneliness, as volunteers meet new people and work together toward a common goal. Studies have shown that people who volunteer regularly report higher levels of life satisfaction and happiness than those who don't.

Volunteering also has physical health benefits. People who volunteer tend to be more physically active, especially if their volunteer work involves physical activity like building houses, cleaning up parks, or coaching sports teams. Studies have found that regular volunteering is associated with lower blood pressure, reduced risk of heart disease, and even longer life expectancy. This is especially true for older adults, for whom staying active and socially engaged is particularly important for health.

In addition to health benefits, volunteering can also help people develop new skills and advance their careers. Volunteers learn practical skills like project management, teamwork, leadership, and communication—skills that are valuable in almost any job. Volunteering can also help people explore new career fields and gain experience in areas they're interested in, which can be especially helpful for students and people looking to change careers.

Volunteering also strengthens communities. When people come together to work on common goals, they build social capital and make their communities stronger and more resilient. Volunteer work fills gaps that government and business can't always fill, supporting everything from education to the arts to social services.

Of course, the main reason people volunteer is to help others and make a positive difference. But it's nice to know that while you're helping others, you're also helping yourself. It's a win-win situation.

There are volunteer opportunities for every interest and schedule, whether you want to volunteer once a week, once a month, or just once in a while. From tutoring children to serving food at a soup kitchen to helping out at an animal shelter to cleaning up a local park, there's something for everyone.

24. How can volunteering help with career development?
